headline: Ebola Deaths Surpass 1,700 as Aid Workers Abandon Fight Over Unpaid Wages
deck: Eastern Congo’s Ebola outbreak is spreading faster than ever while health workers walk out, leaving containment efforts in tatters.
body: The Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has killed more than 1,700 people and shows no sign of slowing, the World Health Organization warned this week. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the virus is spreading faster than response teams can contain it, as health workers abandon their posts over unpaid wages and deadly risks. The Bundibugyo virus, a rare and deadly strain of Ebola, is driving the crisis, complicating containment efforts that were already struggling against armed conflict and mistrust in affected communities.

The strike by aid workers has crippled the response, with health personnel refusing to report to clinics and treatment centers in protest of months of unpaid salaries. Local health officials confirmed that dozens of medical staff have already walked out, while others threaten to join the strike unless their demands are met within days. Without these workers, contact tracing, safe burials, and patient care grind to a halt—directly fueling the virus’s spread.

The scale of the outbreak dwarfs previous Ebola crises in Congo, with fatalities now exceeding 1,700 since the epidemic began in August 2018. Reuters analysis shows the current spread is significantly faster than the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak and the 2018-2019 DRC epidemic. Health experts attribute the acceleration to widespread community resistance, porous borders, and a lack of trust in health authorities—a toxic mix that has repeatedly sabotaged containment in eastern Congo.

In a stark warning, the WHO chief said the situation is spiraling beyond control unless urgent action is taken. ‘The virus is moving faster than we can react,’ Tedros said in a press briefing. ‘We are at a critical juncture where every delay in response costs lives.’ His remarks underscore the dire consequences of the aid worker strike, which has left entire districts without medical oversight.

The strike itself stems from a breakdown in funding and compensation. Many health workers have not received salaries for months, despite risking their lives in one of the world’s most dangerous outbreak zones. CNN reports that some workers have resorted to selling personal protective equipment to feed their families, leaving them—and their communities—exposed to the virus.

Local leaders in Beni and Butembo, two of the worst-hit cities, say the strike has already led to a spike in unreported cases. ‘We are seeing bodies in homes that we cannot safely collect,’ said a local health coordinator who asked to remain anonymous. ‘Families are burying their dead without protection, and the virus is spreading silently.’

The crisis is unfolding against a backdrop of chronic instability in eastern Congo, where armed groups and state forces vie for control. Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that violence and displacement are hampering access to remote villages, where the virus thrives. The strike only deepens the vulnerability of those cut off from help.

WHO officials are now racing to secure emergency funds to restart operations, but the window for containment is closing. ‘We need health workers on the ground now,’ said a senior WHO official. ‘Without them, this outbreak will not just continue—it will explode.’
